brief.head: The tank and the robot
brief.text: Early en­gines won by brute force. Kasparov, Amit Varma said, likened it to want­ing a robot to climb Everest and get­ting a tank that rolled up. {052-C03}

brief.head: A civilised game
brief.text: Chess has an open cat­e­gory, not a men’s one, Amit Varma said. Unlike poker’s hos­tile ta­bles, it is “a beau­ti­ful civ­i­lized world with re­ally de­cent peo­ple”. {052-C16}

brief.head: A champion in a pocket
brief.text: Every mo­bile phone can now beat the world cham­pion, a friend told Ajay Shah. What sad­dens him is how lit­tle peo­ple do with this mir­a­cle. {052-S15}

brief.head: Real but overblown
brief.text: Cheating is an enor­mous threat but an overblown one, Amit Varma said. Top events use metal de­tec­tors, closed halls and a 20-minute broad­cast delay. {052-S14}

brief.head: Number one, briefly
brief.text: Amit Varma plays vari­ants such as Atomic Chess and Fog of War, where heuris­tics fail. In a cou­ple he was briefly num­ber one on chess.com[[x4]]. {052-S21}

thought.label: Thought for the day

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the game they both love
lead.head: Board games and power games

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 52

body: Amit Varma played se­ri­ous chess in col­lege until he was nine­teen. Then he re­tired, he said, when he re­alised that he could not be an Anand: in the early 1990s, below Anand’s level, you could not make a liv­ing from the game. {052-S01}

He never stopped fol­low­ing it. Chess is one of the three sports he tracks most closely, and in this episode, which Ajay Shah in­tro­duced as the fourth of their “beer ses­sions”, Varma told its story.

The oc­ca­sion was D Gukesh reach­ing the world cham­pi­onship match[[x1]]. For many Indians that is a na­tion­al­is­tic thing, Varma said, and a good rea­son to cel­e­brate. He wanted to add the his­tory and the con­text.
## The price of a title

For decades, the title be­longed partly to who­ever could pay for it. After Wilhelm Steinitz be­came the first widely ac­cepted cham­pion in 1886, any strong player who could raise the money for a match could chal­lenge. {052-S02}

Champions wrote rules that suited them­selves. Emanuel Lasker wanted a chal­lenger to win by two points. Under FIDE, Varma ar­gued, Mikhail Botvinnik gained from a cap on en­trants per coun­try, which lim­ited the strong Soviets who could threaten him.

The Soviet state chose its own he­roes, pre­fer­ring the loyal Anatoly Karpov to the out­spo­ken Garry Kasparov. And a cen­tury after Steinitz, one chal­lenge cycle still col­lapsed be­cause no­body could fund the match.

Behind the Soviet dom­i­nance lay a school. Children were taught chess as they were taught maths, and the best play­ers, Varma said, read pat­terns rather than cal­cu­lat­ing fur­ther ahead. Vishy Anand had none of that train­ing, learned on the fly, and beat the world’s best in his teens.
## Machines and mam­mals

When en­gines over­took hu­mans, many ex­pected them to flat­ten chess into one com­puter style. The op­po­site hap­pened, Varma said. The flat­ten­ing had been done by the Soviet school; en­gines sup­plied con­crete ex­cep­tions to its prin­ci­ples, and play­ers de­vel­oped styles of their own. {052-C04}

AlphaZero, which taught it­self in a day, showed that hu­mans had over­val­ued ma­te­rial against ini­tia­tive. Yet the game is far from solved, and teenagers now sharpen their pat­tern recog­ni­tion by play­ing huge vol­umes of games on­line.
## Chess and the na­tion

Shah then asked what chess says about a coun­try. Not much, he said at first: the USSR ruled the game from Botvinnik to Kasparov and still col­lapsed. India’s rise im­pressed him more be­cause the state did noth­ing to make it.
He tested a de­lib­er­ately ex­treme the­ory, that tal­ent is fixed at con­cep­tion, so that a country’s grand­mas­ters should sim­ply track its pop­u­la­tion. {052-C10}

It fails. India has about 84 grand­mas­ters for some 1,440 mil­lion peo­ple, Shah said, the United States 101 and Russia 236, while Bangladesh and Pakistan, both very large, have had lit­tle suc­cess in chess.

Nurture and com­mu­nity must do the rest: a fam­ily with money to spare for what Shah called “the silli­ness”, an early start, and par­ents who will travel to tour­na­ments rather than push the child to­wards the JEE.
Varma added that ex­cel­lence comes in clus­ters, often seeded by ac­ci­dent, and that India as a whole is the wrong unit.

Shah’s cau­tion was about am­bi­tion. Chess needs a richer cul­ture than cricket, he said, but lead­er­ship, in­no­va­tion and lit­er­a­ture need far more. “Just be­cause you’ve got 84 he­roes who are grand­mas­ters, it doesn’t take you to 84 poets.” {052-C14}
At the very end, the two of them sat down to play a game.

second.label: Computer chess
second.head: All brain, no machine
second.deck: In 1948 Alan Turing designed a chess program that no computer could run

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Turing’s paper engine

body: In 1948, Amit Varma said, Alan Turing and David Champernowne cre­ated a chess pro­gram called Turochamp. It was an al­go­rithm on paper, and no com­puter then, or for some time after, was pow­er­ful enough to run it. {052-S09}

So it could never be tested. Turing died “too young and too trag­i­cally”, in Varma’s words, and Champernowne aban­doned the project. Only after Moore’s Law kicked in did pro­cess­ing power catch up with such ideas.

Progress, when it came, was slow. Ken Thompson, an­other of Ajay Shah’s he­roes[[x2]], built Belle, the world com­puter cham­pion in the early 1980s, which reached about 2,200 Elo. That, Varma ad­mit­ted, is “stronger than me today”. {052-J12}

quote.text: So it is just an al­go­rithm on paper that they have cre­ated, but they can never re­ally test it.

third.head: Taught in the nursery

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Devangshu Datta’s Soviet lesson

body: Devangshu Datta, a friend of both hosts, played chess se­ri­ously in the 1980s. As a young player he would sweat through the open­ing and the mid­dlegame against Soviet op­po­nents[[x3]], spend 40 min­utes on a sin­gle move, and still lose. {052-S07}
Then, he told Amit Varma, the Soviet player would ask what he had been cal­cu­lat­ing. “It is taught to us in nurs­ery that in this kind of for­ma­tion you play like this.”
There was no in­ter­net and no data­base in those days, Varma said, so play­ers from other coun­tries had to work all of it out for them­selves.
Ajay Shah’s favourite chess-book phrase cap­tures the same gap. A deep in­sight, such as that the king is an at­tack­ing piece, would be pref­aced with “as every Russian school­boy knows”. {052-J09}

box.title: The boy who solved too much
box.text: India’s first grand­mas­ter learned with­out the Soviet ma­chine[[x7]]. As a boy in the Philippines, Amit Varma said, Vishy Anand kept crack­ing a TV chess programme’s puz­zle of the week, until it told him to stop en­ter­ing. {052-S17}

sections.label: The championship
sections.head: Whoever pays, plays
sections.caption: the history of the world title
body: Chess in the 19th cen­tury was un­or­gan­ised, Amit Varma said. Wilhelm Steinitz be­came the first cham­pion widely ac­cepted by the com­mu­nity when he beat Johannes Zukertort in 1886. Zukertort had fin­ished three points ahead of him at a great tour­na­ment in London in 1883.

There was no gov­ern­ing body, so the rule be­came that any strong chal­lenger who could raise the money got a match. {052-S02} Siegbert Tarrasch had slightly bet­ter re­sults but could not; Emanuel Lasker could, and kept the title for 27 years. {#lasker}

When José Raúl Capablanca came call­ing, Lasker de­manded that the chal­lenger win by two points, or the match would count as a draw and Lasker would keep the crown. Varma called it ridicu­lous, and “a pre­cur­sor to fu­ture rules which are as ridicu­lous”.
## The rule-makers

After Alekhine died in 1945, FIDE took over. Its cycle capped how many play­ers any one coun­try could send, which looked fair, since the Soviets held most of the top spots. But Mikhail Botvinnik, Varma said, was close to the rule-makers, and fewer Soviet en­trants meant fewer com­pa­tri­ots to threaten him. {052-S03} A drawn match let the cham­pion keep his title; a de­posed one got a re­match.
~ The state later picked its own favourite in Anatoly Karpov, “a party man”. In the 1990s, Garry Kasparov broke with FIDE over money for a match, ask­ing where its le­git­i­macy came from. {052-S06}

quote.text: which­ever strong player wishes to chal­lenge me, if they can come up with the fund­ing for the game, I’ll play.

sections.label: The ideas
sections.head: Schoolboys and black boxes
sections.caption: how chess ideas evolved
body: Beginners think tac­ti­cally, Amit Varma said: if I do this, he will do that. Deeper play­ers think strate­gi­cally, and much of that foun­da­tional think­ing is cred­ited to Wilhelm Steinitz.

The Soviet school built a ped­a­gogy on it. Varma cited Adriaan de Groot’s study[[x9]], which he dated to 1942: the best play­ers do not think more moves ahead than am­a­teurs, they are much bet­ter at pat­tern recog­ni­tion. {052-C01} The Soviets for­malised those pat­terns and taught them from child­hood.
## Machines that di­ver­si­fied

Computers, many feared, would flat­ten chess[[x8]], with ev­ery­one play­ing the same moves. The op­po­site hap­pened. The flat­ten­ing, Varma ar­gued, had been done by the Soviet school; en­gines of­fered con­crete ex­cep­tions to its prin­ci­ples, and play­ers began to de­velop styles of their own. {052-C04}
Then came AlphaZero, given no human heuris­tics. Learning by play­ing it­self, it showed, in Varma’s words, “that we were over­valu­ing ma­te­rial in con­trast to ini­tia­tive”. {052-C05}

~ Ajay Shah drew out the change in com­pen­sa­tion. A 19th-century sac­ri­fice was a pre­cise com­bi­na­tion re­paid within a few moves; AlphaZero gives up ma­te­rial for po­si­tion and waits ten or fif­teen moves for a struc­tural pay­off.

quote.text: The op­po­site hap­pens be­cause a great flat­ten­ing sound was the Soviet school of chess.

sections.label: Man and machine
sections.head: Bad moves, good bets
sections.caption: why chess is still a human game
body: Ajay Shah put a friend’s ver­dict to Amit Varma: was chess over? Varma an­swered with an anal­ogy. If bots could per­fectly im­i­tate the two of them, would Shah stop talk­ing to him? {052-C06}

Nor is the game solved. Endgame table­bases give per­fect an­swers[[x11]] only with seven or fewer pieces on the board, en­gines tackle po­si­tions dif­fer­ently, and there is no sin­gle line that draws every game.
## Wrong on pur­pose

At the top, Varma said, the edge comes from de­vi­at­ing. A move that is sub­op­ti­mal against per­fect com­puter play may be ex­cel­lent against a human, whose prepa­ra­tion does not cover it and who must start think­ing, and sec­ond-guessing, at the board. {052-C07}

For a world cham­pi­onship match, the prepa­ra­tion runs to months. Each player works with a team of sec­onds whose names are kept se­cret, be­cause “you pro­file the sec­onds and you can fig­ure shit out”. {052-S12}

~ Magnus Carlsen tired of it all[[x10]]. Rather than give up six months to dreary study, he walked away from the title, telling the chess world to find an­other way. {052-S13} He now plays more rapid, blitz and Chess960, also known as Fischer Random.

quote.text: Will you stop talk­ing to me, Ajay? You won’t, right? The human con­nec­tion mat­ters.

portraits.caption: Magnus Carlsen
portraits.credit: Andreas Kontokanis from Piraeus, Greece, CC BY-SA 2.0

sections.label: The new generation
sections.head: Play more, panic less
sections.caption: chess as a spectator sport
body: Chess has be­come a spec­ta­tor sport, Amit Varma said, and com­men­tary is part of the rea­son. Commentators use en­gines to show the best moves, and grand­mas­ters ex­plain what the play­ers are think­ing. Ajay Shah was taken with events that show the au­di­ence both players’ heart rates[[x12]]. “I think that’s ge­nius,” he said. {052-C09}

Varma saw a par­al­lel with poker, which youth took over once play­ers on­line could play in thirty months the hands Doyle Brunson took thirty years to play. Young chess play­ers now put in the same vol­ume[[x13]], sharp­en­ing their pat­tern recog­ni­tion. {052-C08}
## The calm one

Before the Candidates, Varma saw D Gukesh as high-variance, a player who could win or fin­ish near the bot­tom. He ad­mits he was partly wrong. Gukesh was never out­played and lost only once, to Firouzja, after a blun­der in time trou­ble.
One ex­pla­na­tion, Varma said, is that until he be­came a grand­mas­ter Gukesh did not use com­put­ers. He stud­ied through hu­mans and books, and is super solid on prin­ci­ples. {052-S16}
~ His coach, Grzegorz Gajewski, once Vishy Anand’s sec­ond, mar­vels at how calm he is. Varma has high hopes, though he feels Magnus Carlsen’s ab­di­ca­tion has de­val­ued the title.

quote.text: I just need to take you out of your prep some­how. And then we’ll play and I’ll out­play you, boss.

sections.label: Nature and nurture
sections.head: Turning the knobs
sections.caption: what chess says about a nation
body: Ajay Shah asked what India’s chess boom says about India. His first an­swer was “a triv­ial de­bat­ing point”. The USSR dom­i­nated chess from Botvinnik to Kasparov and col­lapsed any­way. It was a failed coun­try, he said, and if Russia is good at one thing, it is “ex­port­ing all its tal­ent”. {052-J04}

Even so, Shah re­spects India’s rise more than the Soviet one. The Soviet state fil­tered mil­lions of chil­dren[[x14]] with heavy in­cen­tives, a project in which, as he put it, “some hor­mones were in­jected and some crea­ture was pro­duced”. {052-J05} India’s grand­mas­ters bub­bled up from fam­i­lies while the state did noth­ing.
## The fil­ters
Shah then tested a the­ory that abil­ity is fixed at con­cep­tion[[x15]], so that grand­mas­ters should track pop­u­la­tion. The data re­ject it. {052-C10}

What else counts? The hosts’ friend Ayush reck­ons a fam­ily needs about $5,000 a head to af­ford what Shah called “the silli­ness”. {#ayush} The child must start be­fore ten, with a com­puter, the in­ter­net and coach­ing, and par­ents must be able to travel to tour­na­ments.

~ Amit Varma, quot­ing Steven Pinker, said na­ture gives you knobs and nur­ture turns them. {052-C11} India’s 1.4 bil­lion, he ar­gued, is a mis­lead­ing num­ber: per­haps only 10 to 20 mil­lion peo­ple live where chil­dren get leisure time that is not goal-directed.

quote.text: So you have one clear counter ex­am­ple where ex­treme suc­cess in chess went along with ex­treme and com­pre­hen­sive so­ci­etal and state fail­ure.

sections.label: Chess and India
sections.head: Grandmasters aren’t poets
sections.caption: clusters, poets and lunchrooms
body: Does hav­ing 84 grand­mas­ters mean India can have 84 poets? Not so fast, Ajay Shah said. {052-C14}

He laid out a spec­trum. Cricket and the IPL need a sim­pler pack­age of skills; chess needs some­what more cul­ture and com­mu­nity; lead­er­ship, in­no­va­tion and lit­er­a­ture need far more. India’s ser­vices ex­ports, he said, mostly fill nar­row roles in which a global firm sup­plies the cul­ture and the strat­egy, and the worker can “shut up and turn the wrench”. Few Indian or­gan­i­sa­tions work as tal­ent fac­to­ries, as he con­sid­ers NIPFP and XKDR Forum to be.
## Accidents and clus­ters
Amit Varma was un­easy with India as the unit. You could look at Mylapur, he said, and call it an OECD coun­try. {052-C13}

Excellence comes in clus­ters[[x16]], he ar­gued, often seeded by ac­ci­dent: Anand’s child­hood in the Philippines helped make Tamil Nadu a chess hub. Shah agreed, and pre­dicted many lit­tle cul­tures, of physi­cists and, at Varma’s prompt­ing, pod­cast­ers, each of which could ex­plode.
~ Shah’s test of such a cul­ture is the lunch­room. Where work is just a job, peo­ple dis­cuss Bollywood. As ca­pa­bil­ity grows, ideas take over the lunch table. {052-C15}

quote.text: Little peo­ple talk about peo­ple, medium peo­ple talk about news, great minds talk about ideas.

art.caption: Ajay Shah (left) on clusters, poets and lunchrooms, with Amit Varma

quote.text: We are mam­mals. And we are sub­ject to the foibles of mam­mals, which in­cludes being able to read sub­tle mus­cle tone of each other’s faces, which never hap­pens on a video call.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Rebels, prodigies, machines and wrestlers: the episode’s stories, and what they teach

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the rebel who took the crown and vanished
stories.head: Six-nil, then silence
body: As a teenager, Amit Varma said, Bobby Fischer did not do all that well in the in­ter­zon­als. Soviet play­ers such as Keres, Geller and Tal were re­ally strong. {052-S04}
But he got bet­ter. Varma calls him a prodi­gal tal­ent and “one of the true ge­niuses of the sport”, and a rebel in the sys­tem.
The rebel showed it­self when Fischer de­cided not to play, and so did not qual­ify from the zon­als. Then, Varma said, he de­cided he wanted to play after all.
One by one, the top three American qual­i­fiers dropped out to make room for him. {#dropout} “And all three of them have to drop off for him to take the place, and he does,” Varma said.

He won a can­di­dates match 6-0 against Taimanov. {#sixnil} He won an­other 6-0, de­stroyed the for­mer cham­pion Tigran Petrosian and, after for­feit­ing the first game of a fa­mous match in Reykjavik, beat Boris Spassky for the title. “And you’re like wow,” Varma said.

The Soviet school then pro­duced Anatoly Karpov, who qual­i­fied to chal­lenge him in 1975. Fischer began set­ting bizarre con­di­tions, Varma said, very like those Lasker had once set for Capablanca, such as a two-game gap. Essentially, he did not want to play.

~ He dis­ap­peared from chess, grew a big beard and be­came a recluse, and Karpov took over. “Now we can spec­u­late about why that is,” Varma said. “But he’s reached the high­est level he could have.”
stories.why: Even a lone ge­nius needed three com­pa­tri­ots to step aside be­fore he could climb. At the sum­mit, he reached for the self-serving terms an ear­lier cham­pion had used, and walked away rather than de­fend the crown.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Bobby Fischer’s rise and exit

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on India’s first grandmaster
stories.head: Small car, big race
body: Vishy Anand, Amit Varma said, had none of the Soviet train­ing[[x17]]. He had bril­liant tac­ti­cal sense and learned the rest on the fly. Winning the world cham­pi­onship that way was “like some­one tak­ing a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race and win­ning”. {052-S08}

Behind the image of a nice, con­ven­tional gen­tle­man, Varma said, Anand was an ag­gres­sive, fe­ro­cious player. Then he caught his tense. “And is, in fact,” he added. “I apol­o­gize, Vishy, if you’re watch­ing this.” {052-J02}

When Varma was a teenager there was a race to be­come India’s first grand­mas­ter. Pravin Thipsay earned norms but got stuck, and Dibyendu Barua had fa­mously beaten Korchnoi at twelve. The younger Anand got there first.
~ “I re­mem­ber the days we had zero,” Varma said. India now has 84. {#zero}
stories.why: Anand’s great­ness, Varma sug­gested, is best mea­sured against the in­fra­struc­ture he never had. Having made it with­out the sys­tem, he be­came the hero a whole gen­er­a­tion of Indian play­ers grew up want­ing to be.

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the machine that taught itself chess
stories.head: Centuries of chess in a day
body: AlphaZero, in­spired by AlphaGo, was given no human prin­ci­ples or heuris­tics, Amit Varma said. It sim­ply played chess against it­self[[x18]] for 24 hours. {052-S10}

In that time it re­traced the game’s his­tory. It was taken with the French Defence, then de­cided it was a lit­tle in­fe­rior, much as hu­mans did. It dis­cov­ered the Berlin Defence, which Kramnik re­vived to beat Kasparov in the early 2000s.
Then it went be­yond[[x19]]. In a match against Stockfish, then the strong­est brute-force en­gine, it cal­cu­lated a tenth or a hun­dredth as much, and still de­stroyed it. {#tenth}
~ What it had learned stayed in a black box, Varma said. Nobody knows what prin­ci­ples it dis­cov­ered for it­self; we know only that they work.
stories.why: Centuries of human wis­dom were re­dis­cov­ered, then sur­passed, in a sin­gle day. Principles held for gen­er­a­tions can be sound and still wrongly weighted: hu­mans, the ma­chine showed, had been over­valu­ing ma­te­rial against ini­tia­tive. {052-C05}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on AlphaZero’s day of self-play

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how an accident made a cluster
stories.head: Wrestling with an accident
body: Haryana, Amit Varma said, is known to be very bad for its women in most ways. Yet it has a lot of women wrestlers. {052-C13}
It goes back to the late 1970s and a wrestler called Chandgi Ram. Wrestlers trained their sons to fol­low them, but he had no son, only a daugh­ter, Sonika Kaliraman.

Then, in an ac­ci­dent of his­tory, the Olympics opened up women’s wrestling. {#olympics} His eyes lit up, Varma said, and he trained his girl. His as­sis­tant, Mahavir Singh Phogat, trained his own three daugh­ters, whose story be­came the film *Dangal*. “So an ac­ci­dent of his­tory cre­ated a clus­ter,” Varma said. {052-S19}
~ India’s chess boom, he ar­gued, is like­wise one lit­tle clus­ter within India, not India it­self.
stories.why: Clusters of ex­cel­lence often begin when one person’s cir­cum­stance meets a change in the rules, Varma ar­gued, rather than with any re­gional virtue. That is why he prefers the clus­ter to the coun­try as the unit.

quiz.q: Why did Amit Varma stop playing serious chess at nineteen, in the early 1990s?
quiz.a: He re­alised he couldn’t be an Anand, and only Anand’s level paid a liv­ing.

quiz.q: Before FIDE, what did a challenger need in order to play the world champion?
quiz.a: The fund­ing: any strong player who could raise the money got a match.

quiz.q: What did Adriaan de Groot’s study find about how the best players think?
quiz.a: They don’t cal­cu­late fur­ther ahead; they are far bet­ter at pat­tern recog­ni­tion.

quiz.q: How long did AlphaZero play against itself before it relived all of chess history?
quiz.a: Twenty-four hours, re­dis­cov­er­ing the French and Berlin Defences along the way.

quiz.q: Which wrestler, wanting a son to train, started Haryana’s cluster of women wrestlers?

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 52. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Bobby Fischer (Bert Verhoeff for Anefo, CC0); Viswanathan Anand (Wolfgang Jekel, CC BY 2.0); Wilhelm Steinitz (Schumann, Fritz, public domain); Emanuel Lasker (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 de); Magnus Carlsen (Andreas Kontokanis from Piraeus, Greece, CC BY-SA 2.0); Gukesh D (Frans Peeters, CC BY-SA 2.0); Steven Pinker (Christopher Michel, CC BY-SA 4.0); Garry Kasparov (Lukasz Kobus, CC BY 4.0); Hikaru Nakamura (Andreas Kontokanis from Piraeus, Greece - photo DS28 - crop., CC BY-SA 2.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Game Changer
shelf.creator: Matthew Sadler and Natasha Regan
shelf.why: It shows which human heuris­tics AlphaZero’s play forces us to re­think, such as ma­te­rial ver­sus ini­tia­tive and play down the flanks, and Amit says it will make you a bet­ter player.

shelf.title: How Life Imitates Chess
shelf.creator: Garry Kasparov
shelf.why: Amit con­sid­ers Kasparov a great mind, and hopes he suc­ceeds in ‘the larger game that he is playing’.

shelf.title: GothamChess
shelf.creator: Levy Rozman
shelf.why: He builds human drama into the anal­y­sis and makes you feel you un­der­stand chess like an ex­pert.

shelf.title: agadmator’s Chess Channel
shelf.creator: agadmator
shelf.why: He plays through clas­sic games and talks about them, which Amit finds won­der­ful.

shelf.title: Hikaru Nakamura’s channel
shelf.creator: Hikaru Nakamura
shelf.why: He plays bul­let game after game for five or six hours while ex­plain­ing his think­ing, which is fan­tas­tic and in­struc­tive.

shelf.title: ChessBase India
shelf.creator: Sagar Shah and Amruta
shelf.why: Sagar Shah and Amruta Mokal’s chess plat­form, which began as a labour of love (cov­er­ing ob­scure tour­na­ments, in­ter­view­ing play­ers, analysing games) and pi­o­neered using com­put­ers to il­lu­mi­nate the game.

shelf.title: The Dream Becomes a Reality
shelf.creator: Sagar Shah
shelf.why: Gukesh ex­plains how he plays an un­usual but not bad move order so that op­po­nents must start think­ing for them­selves and won­der whether he has se­cret prep.

shelf.title: Atomic Chess and Fog of War
shelf.why: Your usual heuris­tics, in­stincts and even pat­tern recog­ni­tion stop work­ing, so you have to work out how to play from first prin­ci­ples.

shelf.title: Thought and Choice in Chess
shelf.creator: Adriaan de Groot
shelf.why: De Groot’s find­ing that grand­mas­ters look no fur­ther ahead than novices but excel at pat­tern recog­ni­tion, which un­der­pins Amit’s ac­count of why the Soviet school dom­i­nated chess.

shelf.title: The Tamilian Gentleman Who Took on the World
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s piece on Viswanathan Anand ris­ing with­out the Soviet school’s sys­tem­atic train­ing, like tak­ing a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race, which shows how ex­tra­or­di­nary his world-championship ca­reer was.

shelf.title: The Seen and the Unseen episode with Devangshu Datta
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A life-and-times con­ver­sa­tion with the hosts’ friend Devangshu Datta, from chess and his Brahmo Samaj back­ground to a fam­ily tree with three great-grandfathers who had in­sti­tu­tions named after them and a fourth who was a river pi­rate in Bengal.

shelf.title: Magnus Carlsen Ranks The Candidates Players
shelf.creator: Magnus Carlsen
shelf.why: Amit felt Carlsen broadly got it right but missed that some play­ers, Gukesh among them, had high ceil­ings and high vari­ance.

shelf.title: Poker and Life (Episode 38)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: What Amit’s five years as a pro­fes­sional poker player taught him about life: most of what hap­pens is luck, so don’t let suc­cess go to your head or fail­ure crush you, and focus on doing the right things.

shelf.title: Range Rover
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: The ar­chive of the poker col­umn Amit wrote for the Economic Times, in which he ap­plied poker’s prob­a­bilis­tic think­ing be­yond the table: the full body of his poker writ­ing for read­ers who want to go deeper.

shelf.title: Om Namah Volume
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: One of Amit’s poker col­umns, on his life les­son to ‘put in volume’: a small edge pays off only over a large sam­ple.

shelf.title: I Play to Play
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s essay on the phi­los­o­phy that guides his life and that he gives every young per­son he ad­vises: the game it­self, not win­ning, is the re­ward.

shelf.title: The Girl From Haryana
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It is the fuller ac­count of how a his­tor­i­cal ac­ci­dent cre­ated the Haryana women’s wrestling clus­ter.

laughs.text: After Ajay’s lav­ish in­tro­duc­tion, Amit opens with: ‘Ajay, I have told you in the past, you have to un­der­sell and overde­liver. Now you have over­sold and we will def­i­nitely un­der­de­liver.’
Amit de­scribes Anand as ‘an ag­gres­sive, fe­ro­cious player’ in the past tense, catches him­self, and cor­rects course: ‘And is, in fact... I apol­o­gize, Vishy, if you’re watch­ing this.’

Ajay on the house­hold con­di­tions chess re­quires: enough in­come for ‘the silliness’, since ‘this is a pure waste of time and life to play chess’. Then comes the mo­ment par­ents get hooked: ‘it’s so cool that my lit­tle seven-year-old snotty lit­tle brat ac­tu­ally beats me in chess.’

Ajay’s ‘triv­ial de­bat­ing point’ against treat­ing chess as proof of na­tional great­ness: the USSR dom­i­nated the game and col­lapsed any­way, and ‘if there is one thing that Russia is good at, it is at ex­port­ing all its tal­ent.’
Ajay con­trasts India’s or­ganic chess rise with the Soviet pro­gramme, a project where ‘some hor­mones were in­jected and some crea­ture was produced’.

As Ajay imag­ines fu­ture clus­ters of physi­cists who hang out and go hik­ing to­gether, Amit chips in ‘Podcasters.’ Ajay runs with it: ‘There will be a clus­ter of pod­cast­ers who hang out to­gether... and it will ex­plode.’

Nikolai Krylenko, the Soviet func­tionary later ex­e­cuted by Stalin in 1938, on politi­cis­ing chess: ‘We must fin­ish once and for all with the neu­tral­ity of chess... We must or­ga­nize shock brigades of chess play­ers and begin im­me­di­ate re­al­iza­tion of a five year plan for chess.’
Capablanca was so el­e­gant and ef­fort­less that some called him ‘the machine’, which Amit notes is ironic in today’s com­puter age.

Kasparov’s ver­dict on Carlsen: he com­bines the best of Fischer and Karpov, Fischer’s dy­namic cre­ativ­ity with Karpov’s boa-constrictor squeeze. Carlsen takes equal po­si­tions and squeezes for 40 or 50 moves until ‘you lose, and you don’t know how you lost’.
Ken Thompson, ‘an­other of your heroes’ as Amit tells Ajay, built Belle, the world com­puter chess cham­pion of the early 1980s at roughly 2200 Elo, which Amit ad­mits is ‘stronger than me today’.
Fabiano Caruana reck­ons Arjun Erigaisi is the most promis­ing of India’s four young stars (Gukesh, Praggnanandhaa, Nihal Sarin and Erigaisi). All four have beaten Carlsen in some for­mat.
